signals.title: Optimized support for Open NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Super VL | Red Hat Developer
signals.excerpt:
Red Hat AI is releasing optimized FP8 and DSpark speculative decoding checkpoints for Nemotron 3.5 Super VL, a 120B multimodal mixture-of-experts (MoE) model built for long-running agents. These checkpoints are designed to double inference throughput on NVIDIA Hopper GPUs without compromising output accuracy.

These optimizations combine FP8 quantization using LLM Compressor with a DSpark speculative decoding model trained using Speculators, delivering substantial inference performance gains while preserving model quality.
...
To accelerate inference for Nemotron 3.5 Super VL, we are releasing an optimized FP8-quantized checkpoint. FP8 quantization reduces the precision of model weights and activations from BF16 to 8-bit floating point, cutting model weight memory and storage requirements in half while preserving model quality.

FP8 quantization is particularly effective on NVIDIA Hopper GPUs, which feature native FP8 Tensor Core support and deliver approximately 2× higher theoretical matrix multiplication throughput compared to BF16. Combined with reduced memory bandwidth requirements, this enables higher inference throughput and improved GPU efficiency, especially for large-scale models.

We generated the quantized checkpoints using the LLM Compressor library and its model-free post-training quantization (PTQ) workflow, leveraging the calibration-free nature of FP8 Dynamic quantization.

After evaluating several quantization configurations, we settled on quantizing the attention, expert, and Mamba projection layers of the main model, while keeping the shared experts, routers, normalization layers, and `lm_head` in their original precision. For the multi-token prediction (MTP) layers, we quantized the attention, expert, and shared expert layers, while leaving the normalization layers and `eh_proj` unquantized.
...
To assess the impact of quantization on model accuracy, particularly in reasoning-intensive tasks and agentic workflows, we evaluate both the BF16 and FP8 models across a broad suite of representative benchmarks. To ensure a fair and consistent comparison, both models are evaluated under identical conditions: non-greedy sampling, four NVIDIA H200 GPUs, vLLM 0.31.0, and the Inspect AI and Harbor evaluation frameworks. The evaluation results are presented in Figure 1. The FP8 checkpoint consistently preserves model accuracy across all evaluated benchmarks.
...
The performance gains from quantized checkpoints can be further extended by enabling speculative decoding with parallel drafting DSpark models. Speculative decoding accelerates inference by using a smaller, faster draft model to propose multiple tokens ahead of time, which the LLM then verifies in parallel.
...
Quantization and speculative decoding are complementary, orthogonal inference acceleration techniques that can be combined to achieve compounded performance gains. To demonstrate their individual and combined impact, we conducted a series of benchmarks using vLLM, highlighting the performance improvements enabled by each optimization and the additional benefits of combining them.

The following plots (Figure 3, Figure 4, and Figure 5) demonstrate performance benchmarking, comparing the performance gains achieved through swapping MTP speculative decoding with our trained DSpark speculator as well as swapping the BF16 checkpoint for our FP8 quantized checkpoint. All benchmarks were performed on four H100s across workloads with prompts from various datasets. Each chart shows per-user streaming speed (interactivity) on the x-axis versus total output throughput (tok/s) on the y-axis, with each point representing a different concurrency level N. The HumanEval prompts come from OpenAI's HumanEval coding benchmark, while the math_reasoning and RAG prompts come from Spec-Bench, the ACL 2024 speculative decoding benchmark suite.

Each upgrade delivers meaningful gains on its own, and they compose cleanly. Swapping MTP for our trained DSpark speculator at BF16 primarily boosts single-user streaming speed, while swapping the BF16 checkpoint for FP8 primarily boosts aggregate throughput under load, where its reduced compute and memory footprint matters most. Combining them outperforms either intermediate configuration at every concurrency level on both workloads.
...

The method, called DualQuant, was posted to arXiv on October 9 by researchers affiliated with d-Matrix, a Santa Clara AI inference chip startup. The framework targets the same W4A4 inference problem as SmoothQuant — compressing both weights and activations to 4-bit precision simultaneously — but requires no representative input data at quantization time. On a real packed W4A4 inference path for Llama-3.1-8B running on an RTX 4090, DualQuant delivered 2.61x memory reduction benchmark results and up to 2.46x throughput speedup over a BF16 baseline while matching SmoothQuant's accuracy. The news comes as the Open Compute Project's annual Global Summit — the standards-setting body for the MXFP4 format that DualQuant targets — runs this week in San Jose.
...
The Open Compute Project Global Summit runs October 12–15, 2026, in San Jose, and it is the institutional home of the Microscaling (MX) format standard — the open specification that defines MXFP4, the 4-bit block floating-point format now supported by AMD's Instinct MI350 series and Intel's forthcoming Xe3P data center GPU. NVIDIA's competing 4-bit format, NVFP4, is natively implemented in Blackwell NVFP4 Tensor Core specs that power the B100, B200, and GB200 series.

Both formats are already in active production deployment. NVIDIA has published NVFP4 checkpoints for DeepSeek models including V3.2 and V4, with DeepSeek V4 Blackwell NVFP4 performance reaching approximately 3,500 tokens per second on Blackwell hardware. AMD's MI355X surpassed one million tokens per second in MLPerf Inference 6.0. Intel's Xe3P architecture — detailed at Hot Chips 2026 in August — supports FP4 and MX microscaling with 480GB of LPDDR5X memory.
...
SmoothQuant (MIT/NVIDIA), the state of the art, addressed this by offline-migrating quantization difficulty from activations to weights via a per-channel scaling transformation. The transformation is computed from a small representative calibration sample — typically 512 to 2,048 input sequences run through the model before deployment. The approach works well enough that it has been incorporated into SmoothQuant TensorRT-LLM production integration and Amazon SageMaker. But it carries a hidden operational cost: for every new model variant, fine-tune, or deployment context, operators must maintain a curated calibration dataset, manage its versioning, and accept the risk that a dataset tuned to one distribution may subtly distort accuracy in another.
...
Research presented at ICLR 2026 established that MXFP4's power-of-two block scaling severely degrades accuracy in a way that prior calibration-based methods were not designed to address. MXFP4 uses 32-element blocks with a shared scale encoded in E8M0 format — meaning the shared exponent is rounded to a power of two. This is intentionally cheaper to implement in hardware — the OCP MX standard achieves roughly 12% relative area savings in tensor cores compared to NVFP4 — but it introduces additional quantization error that simple scaling strategies cannot recover from.

NVFP4, NVIDIA's proprietary format used in Blackwell Tensor Cores, uses 16-element blocks with an E4M3 shared scale that requires a real floating-point multiply — costlier in hardware but more accurate. The two formats are built on different block structures with different scale granularities, and prior dual-scaling methods including SmoothQuant were designed around tensor-level or per-channel quantization schemes that do not map cleanly onto either.

DualQuant's formulation parameterizes the weight-reconstruction problem to match each target format's specific block structure. The authors claim it is the DualQuant first MX NVFP4 method — the first dual-scaling method to formally support both the full MX family and NVIDIA's NVFP4.
...
The researchers evaluated DualQuant across Llama-3.1-8B, Llama-3.1-70B, and Mixtral-8x7B on standard DualQuant benchmark evaluation results, including WikiText-2 perplexity, C4 perplexity, and zero-shot downstream tasks. Across most models and formats, DualQuant matched or exceeded SmoothQuant's accuracy despite having no access to calibration data, and it substantially outperformed other calibration-free baselines. The largest accuracy gains appear specifically on MX and NV block formats — consistent with the claim that the algorithm's format-native formulation gives it an advantage precisely where prior methods were not designed for the block structure.

The hardware validation on the RTX 4090 Ada Lovelace specs delivered 2.61x memory reduction and 2.46x throughput. A clarification is warranted for practitioners targeting Blackwell or AMD MI350: the RTX 4090 is an Ada Lovelace–architecture GPU (2022) that lacks hardware-native FP4 Tensor Cores. The benchmark implements a custom packed W4A4 integer kernel that packs 4-bit values into 8-bit or 16-bit registers — a genuine 4-bit computation path, but via integer packing rather than the E2M1 or E4M3 Tensor Core instructions that Blackwell and MI350 hardware execute. The accuracy parity between this real kernel and the paper's simulated ("fake") quantization results is meaningful — it confirms the algorithm works in hardware — but practitioners should be aware that throughput benchmarks on Blackwell or MI350 with native FP4 Tensor Cores were not reported in the paper. Those results, when they come, may differ.
...
A calibration-free method collapses this to a single offline computation on model weights alone — no dataset, no environment-specific tuning, no versioning. That simplification matters most for teams deploying models that are frequently fine-tuned (where recalibrating after every fine-tune is expensive), for domains where representative input data is proprietary or scarce, and for any workflow targeting multiple hardware backends at once, since DualQuant's single algorithm covers both MXFP4 and NVFP4 targets simultaneously.
...

MXFP4 is an open standard defined by the Open Compute Project's Microscaling (MX) specification, supported by AMD, Intel, Qualcomm, Microsoft, and others. It uses 32-element blocks with a power-of-two shared exponent (E8M0), which is efficient to implement in hardware but introduces more quantization error than alternatives. NVFP4 is NVIDIA's proprietary variant used in Blackwell Tensor Cores; it uses 16-element blocks with an E4M3 shared scale that requires a real multiply and achieves higher accuracy at slightly higher hardware cost. DualQuant is the first dual-scaling method formally designed to cover both.

With well-designed quantization, the accuracy hit at W4A4 precision can be made small. DualQuant's paper reports matching SmoothQuant — the calibration-based state of the art — on most tested models including Llama-3.1-8B, Llama-3.1-70B, and Mixtral-8x7B, while substantially outperforming calibration-free baselines. Research from Meta presented at ICML 2026 found that naively applied MXFP4 quantization degrades accuracy by around 10% on average relative to BF16 baselines; DualQuant's format-native formulation is designed specifically to address that gap.

Serving Reflection Beam on vLLM from Day 0 | vLLM Blog

# Serving Reflection Beam on vLLM from Day 0
...
TL;DR: Reflection's Beam is a 501B-parameter MoE with 23B active parameters per token. vLLM supports it from day 0 and optimizes it on NVIDIA Blackwell:

- Full feature support. Reasoning, tool calling, and structured outputs work out of the box, and you can run the model with tensor, data, or expert parallelism.
- Agent-driven optimization. Coding agents optimized the model autonomously, making batch-1 decode 2.71× faster and prefill 1.87× faster than our first implementation.
- DFlash2 with adaptive verification. With Beam's DFlash2 drafter, a single request reaches 708 tokens/s on TP8, with an acceptance length of 3.7. Adaptive verification, which decides each step how many draft tokens are worth verifying, adds 10% more throughput at high concurrency.

To try it, use our Docker image `vllm/vllm-openai:reflection-beam`:
...
```
docker run --gpus all --ipc=host -p 8000:8000 \
  -v ~/.cache/huggingface:/root/.cache/huggingface \
  vllm/vllm-openai:reflection-beam \
  reflection/Beam-1.0-501B-A23B-NVFP4 \
  -tp 4 \
  --max-num-seqs 128 \
  --reasoning-parser beam \
  --tool-call-parser beam --enable-auto-tool-choice \
  --kv-cache-dtype fp8 \
  --attention-config '{"backend":"FLASHINFER"}' \
  --kernel-config '{"enable_flashinfer_autotune":false}' \
  --speculative-config '{
    "method": "dflash",
    "model": "reflection/Beam-1.0-501B-A23B-DFlash2",
    "num_speculative_tokens": 7,
    "attention_backend": "FLASH_ATTN"
  }'
...
Beam is a 52-layer MoE decoder with hidden size 5120. The MoE routing follows DeepSeek-V3. The main differences are in the attention layers and in how the residual stream is normalized.
...
Our initial version of implementation was an unoptimized, almost pure PyTorch version of the model. We then optimized it autonomously with coding agents: they profiled the model, wrote the kernels, and benchmarked each change. On TP8, the seven changes below brought batch-1 decode from 8.95 ms to 3.30 ms per step, and an 8 × 2K prefill from 328 ms to 176 ms.
...
In the high concurrency region, Beam's performance can be further improved by combining Attention DP with MegaMoE, powered by FlashInfer's CuTe DSL NVFP4 MegaMoE kernel. The Finalize + norm boundary fusion remains applicable.

| Configuration | Peak input token throughput |
| --- | --- |
| Attention DP + MegaMoE | 168.8K tokens / second |
| ... (`flashinfer_trtllm`, `flashinfer_nvlink_ ... _sided`) | 98.7K tokens / second |

Attention DP with MegaMoE delivered 1.71× higher peak prefill throughput than TP4. Benchmark setup: 4×GB300, with an input sequence length of 32K tokens and an output sequence length of 1 token to isolate prefill performance.
...
## DFlash2 speculative decoding

Beam ships with a DFlash2 draft head, which vLLM supports from day 0. Instead of drafting one token at a time, it predicts a whole block of tokens in a single forward pass from the target model's hidden states.
...
- Adaptive verification. With `"enable_adaptive_verification": true`, vLLM predicts how likely each draft token is to be accepted and verifies only the ones worth their cost, instead of a fixed number per step. DFlash2 has no confidence head, so the acceptance estimate comes from the drafter's own logits (see our recent post on adaptive verification).
- Kernels. The drafter's convolution, norms, and KV writes are fused, and the whole draft step runs in a CUDA graph. FP8 KV cache works for the drafter too, ... no change in acceptance.

Serving results on TP8, with and without adaptive verification, on the low-entropy category of SPEED-Bench's `throughput_1k` split: ~1K-token prompts, mostly code completion and text sorting, with greedy decoding and up to 4K output tokens. Low-entropy text is easier to predict, so expect lower acceptance on open-ended chat.

| Concurrency | Fixed draft (tok/s) | Adaptive (tok/s) | Change | Acceptance length |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 708 | 707 | −0.1% | 3.71 → 3.61 |
| 8 | 3,232 | 3,221 | −0.3% | 3.67 → 3.57 |
| 32 | 7,744 | 8,275 | +6.9% | 3.68 → 3.29 |
| 128 | 15,012 | 16,632 | +10.8% | 3.68 → 3.23 |

Adaptive verification pays off under load. At concurrency 128 it raises output throughput by 10.8% and cuts p99 TPOT by 9%, while verifying fewer draft tokens per step, which lowers acceptance length slightly but saves more compute than it loses. At low concurrency, where extra draft tokens are nearly free, it is neutral.

## AgentX benchmark
...
We also tested Beam on AgentX, which replays multi-turn coding conversations to measure serving performance. With DFlash2, vLLM reached approximately 88K total tokens/s per GPU at 96 concurrent requests. Total throughput counts input and output tokens, including cached input. Input-token cache hit rates ranged from 91.4% to 95.6% across the sweep.

AgentX benchmark configuration: Beam 1.0 NVFP4 on 4× GB300 with TP4/EP1 and FP8 KV cache for both target and drafter. DFlash2 uses real acceptance (average AL 3.6 across measured points), block size 8, and probabilistic sampling. AgentX uses trajectory ratios 0.55–0.75, maximum reasoning effort, temperature 1.0, and 20 minutes per point. Total throughput includes cached input tokens. Source commits: vLLM 8e0922.
...
The command at the top of this post is a good default: TP4 on a single GB300 node, with DFlash2 and FP8 KV cache. To enable adaptive verification, add `"enable_adaptive_verification": true` to the `--speculative-config`. Other optimizations above are on by default.
...
- For the lowest latency, use TP4 or TP8.
- For higher throughput, use data-parallel attention with expert parallelism, e.g. `-dp 4 --enable-expert-parallel`.
- Reasoning and tool calling. The `beam` parsers read the response template that ships with the checkpoint. By default, vLLM also constrains every response to that template, so tool calls always parse and match each tool's JSON schema. `response_format` and `thinking_token_budget` work as usual. To turn the default constraint off, set `VLLM_BEAM_ALWAYS_CONSTRAIN_OUTPUT=0`.
...
We also collaborated with the SkyRL team to enable Day 0 support for RL on Beam. LoRA, BF16 full fine-tuning and MXFP8 RL are supported out of the box, with an upgraded RL stack for the 500B scale.

The SkyRL team post-trained the Beam model on the DAPO recipe with vLLM for inference and Megatron for training. LoRA, full fine-tuning and MXFP8 RL achieve similar gains in performance in 50 training steps, or 100 optimizer updates (reasoning `minimal`), with an average accuracy (avg@8) jump from ~61% to ~79% on AIME25. Average absolute log-probability difference between Megatron and vLLM stays under 0.01 with Rollout Routing Replay (R3) enabled for LoRA and BF16 full fine-tuning, and under 0.03 for MXFP8 RL.

# Welcome Muse Spark Open: open-weight frontier multimodal mixture-of-experts model from Meta 

Published October 15, 2026 

Pedro Cuenca

Muse Spark Open is an open-weight model from Meta. The mixture of experts model brings text, images, audio, and video into a model with approximately 816 billion parameters, around 42 billion active per token, and a context window of up to one million tokens. It generates text, giving developers a common interface for asking questions about different kinds of input.

Following Muse Glimmer, Muse Spark Open introduces a mixture-of-experts architecture at a much larger scale, and the most capable US open-weights model to date.

Meta trained Muse Spark Open for agentic coding: reading a codebase, writing and debugging code, and calling tools. It also takes images, audio, and video as input, so the same model can read a screenshot, listen to a voice note, or watch a screen recording while it works on your code. This post shows you how to run it, how to fine-tune it, and what we built with it. Find all the models here.
...
Meta describes Muse Spark Open as a coding-optimized model trained on real developer workflows such as multi-file refactors and long debugging sessions. Muse Spark Open is an agentic focused model that plans, acts, observes, and self-corrects over long tasks, including browsing the web with images.

| Feature | Muse Spark Open |
| --- | --- |
| Model size | ~816B total parameters; ~42B active per token |
| Expert routing | 256 experts per MoE layer; 8 selected per token |
| Inputs | Text, images, audio, and video |
| Output | Text |
| Context window | Up to 1M tokens |
| Checkpoint formats | BF16 and NVFP4 |
...
Muse Spark Open is the full-size model of the Muse series of models. Muse Glimmer, which Meta released in August, is a small dense model from the same series, ideal for running locally. Both models use the same tokenizer and vocabulary. The chat template follows the Muse Glimmer template, with additions for the new modalities. In Muse Spark Open the input embedding and the output layer are separate matrices of about 1.66B parameters each.
...
Muse Glimmer uses one dense feed-forward network in each layer. Muse Spark Open replaces this dense network with a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) block. Each MoE block has 256 experts, and a router selects 8 experts for each token. Each expert is a feed-forward network that projects from 8192 to 4096 dimensions and back to 8192, then applies its own normalization to its output. The experts hold ~97% of the total model parameters.

Only 8 experts run per token, so the model computes each token with about 42B parameters. All 256 experts stay in memory, so deployment needs the memory of an 816B-parameter model, but runs at the much faster speed of a 42B model. The BF16 checkpoint is about 1.5 TB in safetensors format. The NVFP4 checkpoint stores the parameters in 4-bit precision with negligible loss in accuracy, specifically for NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs. In transformers, the BF16 checkpoint runs across 4 nodes of 8 H200 GPUs with tensor parallelism (TP=32) and the NVFP4 runs on a single B200 node. If you want to deploy Muse Spark Open, check out the `llama.cpp`, vLLM, and SGLang recipes below.
...
The context window is 1M tokens at inference. The configuration sets `max_position_embeddings` to 1,048,576. This includes image, video, and audio tokens in the same window as text.
...
The Muse Spark Open implementation provides `MuseSparkForConditionalGeneration` for text generation from multimodal inputs and `MuseSparkProcessor` for preparing conversations. The processor combines the tokenizer, image and video processors, audio feature extractor, and chat template.

Use a `DistributedConfig` to configure the parallelism settings. `tp_size` is the number of devices across which the dense layers are sharded, and `ep_size` is the number of devices across which the experts are distributed.

The repository containing quants is here. Once the server has started, you can head to localhost:9931 to chat with the built-in WebUI. You can fine-tune the 816B checkpoint with the TRL `SFTTrainer`. This section shows how we fine-tuned it with TRL on 8 nodes of 8 H100 GPUs. The recipe trains LoRA adapters on the attention layers. The experts stay frozen. The full script is in the TRL examples.

# Footnote: Agentic RAG with Sentence-Level Citations - DEV Community
...
An AI research agent for your documents. It decides what to search for, searches again when the results are thin, and every claim in its answer links to the exact sentence it came from.
The usual 'chat with your documents' build searches once with the user's words and hopes. A two-part question gets one search and half an answer. footnote replaces that fixed pipeline with an agent that works like a researcher, built around one rule: an answer you cannot check is not an answer.

Claude is given two tools, `search\_handbook` and `read\_page`, and loops until it can answer. Search results come back as sentence-level blocks, so every citation is validated by the API rather than typed by the model. ...
**Plans its own research.** A two-part question gets two searches, worded the way the handbook words things. Each step shows live in a side panel.
**Sentence-level citations.** Click a citation chip and the source passage scrolls into view with the exact sentence highlighted.
**Says when it doesn't know.** If nothing relevant turns up after retrying, it says the documents don't cover it instead of guessing.
**Swappable search.** Run the agent on hybrid, keyword-only or vector-only search, with each passage's rank in both shown.
...
Python with FastAPI and a one-file HTML UI, Claude through the Anthropic SDK with no framework, and a CLI that prints each tool call. The screenshots come from a keyless demo mode where the model's turns are scripted and the searches and citations run for real.
Retrieval is the easy half. The hard half is making every sentence of the answer checkable.

LocalRAG allows a user to upload documents and ask questions against them.
...
1. Upload a PDF, DOCX, TXT, or Markdown document.
2. Parse and split the document into chunks.
3. Generate embeddings with a local `bge-m3` model.
4. Store vectors in Qdrant.
5. Embed the user's question.
6. Retrieve the most relevant chunks.
7. Generate an answer with a local LLM.
8. Return the answer with source references.
The application does not call a cloud AI API at runtime.
Initial installation still requires network access to pull Docker images and Ollama models. After that, the stack can run inside a local or air-gapped environment.

signals.excerpt:

...
# NVIDIA Details Nemotron 3 Ultra NVFP4 Quantization with Mixed Precision and Four-over-Six Scaling

NVIDIA explains how it quantized Nemotron 3 Ultra to NVFP4, cutting model size from 1,121 GB to 352.3 GB. The post details mixed-precision layer assignments, four-over-six block scaling, and AutoQuantize's bit budget search.
...
NVIDIA published a detailed walkthrough of how it created the Nemotron 3 Ultra NVFP4 checkpoint using NVIDIA Model Optimizer. The quantized model drops from 1,121 GB in BF16 to 352.3 GB, a 3.2x compression that NVIDIA says cuts the hardware footprint in half while matching BF16 accuracy on nearly every benchmark. The post also claims up to 5.9x higher inference throughput than GLM-5.1 754B FP4 on decode-heavy workloads, though that figure is a vendor claim rather than an independent measurement.
...
A key point in the post is that not every layer in the checkpoint is stored in NVFP4. NVIDIA assigned different precisions based on each layer's sensitivity to quantization. The MoE routed experts use NVFP4, while shared experts and Mamba projections use FP8 per-tensor. Attention linears, latent MoE layers, embedding, output classification, and MTP layers stay in BF16. The KV cache is FP8, and the Mamba SSM cache is FP16 with stochastic rounding.

This mixed-precision design lets a single checkpoint run on both Hopper and Blackwell GPUs. On Hopper, which lacks native FP4 tensor cores, the serving framework converts to W4A16. On Blackwell, it uses native W4A4. NVIDIA says W8A8 would be the obvious Hopper choice but leaves too little memory headroom for Multi-Token Prediction, so W4A16 is the better fit.
...
The post walks through several scale-selection methods for FP4 quantization. Max scaling, also called absmax, sets the scale from the block's largest value, but a single outlier can compress other values toward zero. MSE scaling searches for the scale that minimizes average reconstruction error, but NVIDIA found lower MSE did not always improve downstream accuracy. In Nemotron 3 Ultra experiments, MSE calibration cut per-tensor weight error by 27.1% over four-over-six scaling yet produced no consistent benchmark gains.
...
NVFP4 represents only eight positive values: 0, 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, 3, 4, and 6. The gap between 4 and 6 causes aggressive rounding for weights in that range, sometimes over 13% error on a single value. Four-over-six scaling lets each weight block independently choose between a maximum of M=4 or M=6, whichever minimizes reconstruction error. It applies to weights and falls back to default NVFP4 on activations.

NVIDIA used four-over-six to set the FP4 routed-expert weight scales in Nemotron 3 Ultra. It raised the global per-tensor weight scale by 1.75x, and across all 49,152 projection weights in the model's 48 MoE expert layers, it cut median reconstruction MSE by 16.4% compared to standard max calibration. In the balanced 5.03-BPE setting, four-over-six delivered 98.5% median recovery relative to BF16, ahead of max scaling at 96.8% and MSE at 98.4%.
...
NVIDIA Model Optimizer's AutoQuantize searches per-layer format assignments under a target bit budget. The search identified 5.03 effective bits-per-element as the sweet spot where AA-LCR accuracy plateaus after a 2.4-point gain. The NVFP4_FOUR_OVER_SIX_CFG configuration will be released in Model Optimizer 0.46 in July.

For the quantization process itself, NVIDIA used distributed quantization with Megatron-LM on 16 B300 GPUs, reducing total processing time from 120 minutes to 45 minutes versus a Hugging Face Transformers path. The setup used expert and data parallelism with EP=DP=16 for calibration.

Developers can try the recipes via the Model Optimizer launcher, including the Nemotron 3 Ultra YAML recipe for automated quantization and export on a Slurm cluster.

candidates.angle: Developers can now build fully self-hosted Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) stacks using local embeddings (e.g., bge-m3), open-source vector databases (Qdrant), and local LLMs, completely eliminating dependencies on cloud AI APIs for enhanced privacy and cost control.
candidates.audience_pain: Reliance on cloud AI APIs for RAG introduces data privacy concerns and recurring costs, while desiring full control over the entire RAG pipeline for sensitive or custom applications.
candidates.why_now: The emergence of comprehensive open-source projects like LocalRAG demonstrates a practical and verified blueprint for achieving cloud-independent RAG systems.
candidates.hook_seed: Your RAG stack needs zero cloud APIs
